:::{#exm-partials-not-continuous}
#### Partial derivatives can exist where a function is not continuous

Let $f : \reals^2 \to \reals$ be

$$
f(\vx) =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{x_1 x_2}{x_1^2 + x_2^2} & \text{if } \vx \ne \vzero, \\
0 & \text{if } \vx = \vzero.
\end{cases}
$$

**Both partial derivatives exist at $\vzero$.**
For $h \ne 0$, $f(h, 0) = \frac{h \cd 0}{h^2 + 0} = 0$, so

$$
\ba
\frac{f(0 + h, 0) - f(0, 0)}{h}
&= \frac{0 - 0}{h}
&& \text{(} f(h, 0) = 0 \text{ and } f(0, 0) = 0 \text{)}
\\
&= 0,
&& \text{(} 0 / h = 0 \text{ for } h \ne 0 \text{)}
\ea
$$

and the limit as $h \to 0$ is $0$: $\deriv{x_1} f(\vzero) = 0$ (@def-partial-derivative).
The same steps with $f(0, h) = 0$ give $\deriv{x_2} f(\vzero) = 0$.

**But $f$ is not continuous at $\vzero$** (@def-continuous-several).
Take $\varepsilon = \tfrac{1}{4}$ and any $\delta > 0$,
and let $t = \delta / 2$ and $\vy = \tp{(t, t)}$.
Then $\norm{\vy - \vzero} = \sqrt{t^2 + t^2} = t \sqrt{2} = \delta / \sqrt{2} < \delta$, but

$$
\ba
\abs{f(\vy) - f(\vzero)}
&= \abs{\frac{t \cd t}{t^2 + t^2} - 0}
&& \text{(} \vy \ne \vzero \text{, since } t > 0 \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{t^2}{2 t^2}
&& \text{(} t^2 + t^2 = 2 t^2 \text{)}
\\
&= \tfrac{1}{2},
&& \text{(cancel } t^2 > 0 \text{)}
\ea
$$

which is more than $\varepsilon = \tfrac{1}{4}$.

The partial derivatives only look along the two coordinate axes, where $f$ is $0$;
along the line $x_1 = x_2$, $f$ is $\tfrac{1}{2}$ everywhere except at $\vzero$.
So partial derivatives existing at a point says little about how $f$ behaves near it.

:::
